name: AQR Capital Management
rationale: AQR runs machine learning in live production: two dedicated ML strategies, Turing Equities and Turing Macro, launched in 2023 and opened to outside capital in 2025, and Bloomberg reported in April 2025 that machine learning powers about a fifth of the trading signals in AQR's flagship multi-strategy fund (company claim, disclosed to the reporter and not independently audited), alongside ML parsing of unstructured text such as earnings-call transcripts and AI-assisted internal coding. Co-founder Cliff Asness has said on the record that AQR now lets the machine decide more, and that AI has taken over the combining and weighting of investment factors he used to do himself — “annoyingly better than me”. Multiple use cases running daily on real capital, publicly championed by the firm's co-founder, clear the scaling bar. Stops short of embedded: no public source shows AQR's org structure redesigned around AI or decisions taken with no human in the loop — Asness describes ceding specific factor-weighting judgments, not the firm's decision architecture, and AQR's own machine-learning publishing is research thought-leadership rather than evidence of firm-wide restructuring. A March 2026 Forbes profile reinforces both sides of the call: machine learning now recalibrates factor weights in real time across research and trading, while firm insiders describe AI as “evolutionary, not revolutionary,” with human input retained. AQR's own Form ADV brochure (filed 2026-03-31) states the firm “currently utilizes machine learning, natural language processing, and other AI Tools in connection with, and in support of, its investment management activities” — T1 regulatory corroboration of the ML/NLP deployment reported by Bloomberg and Forbes.
footnote: Scope call: AQR publishes extensive academic-style research on machine learning in investing (aqr.com Insights, the “Alternative Thinking” series, “Can Machines Learn Finance?”). That publishing is thought-leadership content rather than evidence of internal deployment, so it was excluded from the stage call; the stage rests instead on Bloomberg's reporting of ML-driven signals running in live funds. AQR's pre-2023 quantitative and machine-learning history is long-standing but predates the GenAI window this dashboard covers, so it is context only and never an events entry.

name: Schroders
rationale: Schroders runs several generative-AI tools in day-to-day production across its own investment operations rather than in contained pilots: Genie, its first proprietary GenAI assistant, was rolled out in April 2023 and is used by over 1,000 colleagues across the firm each day (company claim); First Cut, a custom GPT that produces a first-pass company analysis, had adoption above 80% across investment desks and was saving an average of 50 minutes per investor per day as of June 2025 (company claim); ContextAI screens company reports against roughly 200 targeted sustainability questions for Schroders' own portfolios; and GAiiA, an internal-only generative-AI investment analyst, has been in production since June 2024 for Schroders Capital's private-equity due diligence and draft investment memos. Multiple named tools in daily use across desks, described by the firm as central to its active investment process, clear the scaling bar. Stops short of embedded: Schroders states GAiiA operates with "continual and extensive human oversight and control" and that investors "will always need to check carefully the results generated" by First Cut and ContextAI, so no output reaches a decision unreviewed, and the one agentic system disclosed — a multi-agent equity-research assistant built with Google Cloud — was still an explicitly labelled prototype in June 2025, with analysts reviewing every output. No public source shows Schroders' org structure redesigned around AI.
footnote: Scope call: GAiiA is used by Schroders Capital's own private-equity deal team for due diligence and drafting investment memos, so it is Schroders operating its own investment process with AI — not the excluded case of a manager pushing AI into its portfolio companies (METHODOLOGY §1(c)) — and it counts toward the stage. The Google Cloud multi-agent equity-research assistant is described by both parties as a prototype, so it is recorded as an event but carries no weight as production evidence (§4, plans are not stages). Every penetration figure above (1,000+ daily Genie users, >80% desk adoption of First Cut, ~50 minutes saved per investor per day, ~200 sustainability questions) is Schroders' own disclosure, not independently audited or corroborated by any non-Schroders source — which is why confidence is med rather than high.

name: T. Rowe Price
rationale: T. Rowe Price runs internal AI in production across two distinct functions: its investment professionals use Chat TRP — rolled out as "Investor Copilot" within months of the late-2022 arrival of LLMs — alongside predictive analytics and natural language processing applied to tasks such as analyzing earnings calls, while its chief data office has an LLM in live use that applies the firm's own standards and ETL scripts to structure metadata to about 80% before a human finishes the rest, on top of 1,000+ net-new data quality rules and "data quality ratings" scorecards the board approved for data remediation in 2024. AI is a named firm-wide strategic priority with an organization behind it: an August 2026 announcement created a dedicated Investment AI Solutions organization, T. Rowe Price Labs as the enterprise AI innovation hub, and an enterprise AI and model risk governance function reporting to the chief risk officer. Stops short of embedded: the firm's own published position is that "clear boundaries between full automation and human sign-off must be established", its agentic work is explicitly forward-looking — agent-based AI for multi-step workflows is described as experimentation, and low-code agentic remediation of source data as something that "should occur this year" — and no public source shows AI deciding without a human or the org rebuilt around it. Confidence is held at med because the only disclosed penetration figures (more than 130 AI solutions deployed, associate adoption above 70%) were stated on the Q2 2026 earnings call and no official transcript could be retrieved, so firm-wide daily use rests on the shape of the T1/T2 record rather than a citable number.
footnote: Scope and sourcing calls. Excluded as METHODOLOGY §1(a): AI-powered products and features T. Rowe Price offers to clients, advisers and retirement-plan participants, and the client-engagement pillar of the August 2026 AI strategy (Global Distribution AI, led by Sal Dhanani) — that is distribution, not the firm's own investment process. Excluded as §1(b): the firm's AI-as-investment-thesis output — AI thematic market commentary and its technology funds' AI positioning. Excluded as §4 (plans are not stages): the low-code agentic AI layer intended to remediate data issues at source, which T. Rowe Price's global head of data governance describes in future tense. Excluded on tier: the company's own Q2 2026 earnings-call metrics — "more than 130 AI solutions" deployed firm-wide and "associate adoption exceeding 70%" — because every retrievable copy of that transcript is a third-tier republisher (Motley Fool and its Globe and Mail syndication, Zacks/TradingView) and investors.troweprice.com returned ECONNRESET on every attempt, so no official transcript could be read. Those figures are the single thing that would move this row to high confidence.

OpenAI's own March 2026 customer story adds the penetration metric: roughly 95% of the firm's ~180 investment teams actively use the platform, with named production agents — a Central Bank Speech Analyst that cuts macroeconomic scenario analysis from about two days to roughly 30 minutes, and a Merger Arbitrage Superforecaster that monitors deal probabilities in real time as filings and press releases arrive (company claims, published by OpenAI). No METHODOLOGY §1(a)/(b)/(c) exclusions were needed: no client-facing AI product line and no AI-as-investment-thesis material appeared in the sources read.

name: MacArthur Foundation
aliases: John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation
The John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation
rationale: MacArthur established its first internal policy for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in 2023 and publishes it, and that policy stands up an AI Tool Recommendation and Use Committee (AIRUC), appointed by the President, "responsible for reviewing and approving proposed uses of AI tools" and for maintaining "a use library of AI tools and learnings" — the governance build-out the piloting bar asks for. Real staff usage sits alongside it but stays pocketed: the foundation names analysing its own standard operating procedures to find bottlenecks, reformatting large volumes of data to be legible, identifying patterns in data, reviewing archives for overlooked lessons and stories, building chatbots to pressure-test arguments and strategy, and feeding scenario planning, and reports that "most respondents have saved time using AI tools" in a staff survey (company claim — no penetration figure, no daily-use claim, and no named tool is disclosed). Stops short of piloting: MacArthur's own February 2026 account frames the past two years as "guardrails, pilots, and exploration" and puts "connecting governance and operations" in the next two — future tense, which METHODOLOGY §4 reads as intent one stage below where it points — and the AI policy expressly lists "Using AI for grantmaking decisions or evaluation" and "Using AI for hiring decisions or personnel evaluations" among prohibited uses, so AI is fenced out of the foundation's own capital-allocation decision rather than in production across it. No verified numbers on pilot programs, more of a stance and governance document.
footnote: Scope calls. Excluded under METHODOLOGY §1(c): all of MacArthur's substantial external AI work — the AI Opportunity Big Bet grantmaking program, the $500M Humanity AI coalition and its $18M in grants, the Technology in the Public Interest program strategy, and grantees such as Partnership on AI. That is AI the foundation funds others to build and adopt, not AI in its own operations, and none of it moved this stage; the advertised "Director, AI Opportunity" role is likewise a grantmaking post, not an internal AI/ops function. Sourcing limits: both events rest on a single first-tier URL (MacArthur's own dated Perspectives post) and no independent second-tier coverage of the foundation's INTERNAL adoption was found — philanthropy trade press covers only the grantmaking — which is why confidence is "med" rather than "high". The AI policy page itself carries no visible publication or revision date (it says only that the policy was "recently revised"), so it is used here for existence claims and policy text only, never to date an event. Finally, this row rests on foundation-wide operations, not the endowment team specifically: macfound.org/about/investments describes "rigorous analytical research" and ESG factors with no mention of AI, machine learning or data science, so there is no public evidence either way about AI in manager due diligence or portfolio work.

name: PGGM
rationale: PGGM runs AI in production in named pockets with the governance scaffolding going up around it: its customer-contact operation runs a live pipeline in which calls are converted to text by one AI model, automatically summarised by a second, and quality-checked by an automated "LLM judge", and firm-wide tooling has real reach — more than 70% of colleagues have already worked with Microsoft Copilot, 20% use one or more of the over 90 internal AI assistants built so far, and around 700 colleagues use the PGGM Intelligent Agent every month (company claim) — all organised under a named "AI Accelerator" programme of initiatives "designed to embed AI more deeply into daily operations". On the investment side, IPE reported in October 2024 that PGGM uses large language models in ESG, generative AI in forecasting to improve on quant models, and ChatGPT to improve coding, though without any deployment detail. Governance is explicitly still being built: MLflow is in place as a technical model registry for custom models while integration with broader governance processes including EU AI Act compliance is described as a future objective, an ethical framework is in development, and the proof-of-concept phase for LLM trace monitoring closed only in May 2026 "with first use cases". Stops short of scaling: customer service is the only department publicly named as running production models, every disclosed penetration figure is cumulative ("have already worked with") or monthly rather than daily, and PGGM's own dated framing puts it in "this first phase" where "AI mainly acts as a smart assistant", with collaborative and then autonomous AI placed in later phases — future tense, which §4 counts as intent, one stage lower.

name: BCI (British Columbia Investment Management Corporation)
rationale: BCI runs multiple AI use cases in daily production across both its investment and operations functions, and its own executives name it a strategic priority — COO Shauna Lukaitis: "Innovation is fundamental to how we operate as a global asset manager." rationale: Two Franklin Templeton press releases put AI past pilot and into production in different parts of the firm. The November 2025 Wand AI partnership release states that over the past year the firm has been “evolving from pilot programs to production deployments of intelligent agents across multiple departments”, that “the initial implementation focused on priority use cases within the firm’s investment teams”, and quotes Head of AI Platform Vasundhara Chetluru saying the partnership “brings agentic AI out of the lab and into live production” (company claim — both statements are first-party and no independent T1/T2 source corroborates the breadth). In January 2026 the firm launched Intelligence Hub, “a modular, AI-driven distribution platform powered by Microsoft Azure” built on Azure OpenAI in Foundry, Azure AI Search and Azure AI Document Intelligence, to its U.S. Distribution teams, describing it as “a production-ready platform” that “following a multi-month pilot … delivered measurable efficiency improvements, including reduced daily preparation time and a significant increase in value-added client interactions” — two production deployments in two different functions, which is what carries this past piloting. Stops short of embedded: no public source shows AI making investment decisions without a human in the loop or the organisation redesigned around AI, the agents are framed as supporting research and efficiency, and the firm-wide ambition is future tense — “By 2026, Wand-powered agents are expected to be used in key enterprise workflows” — which METHODOLOGY §4 counts as intent, not deployment.
footnote: Scope and sourcing calls. Intelligence Hub is counted because it is tooling Franklin Templeton runs for its own U.S. Distribution staff, not software sold to clients; the firm’s client- and advisor-facing AI-flavoured products and its AI-as-investment-theme commentary are excluded under METHODOLOGY §1(a) and §1(b) and did not move the stage. If any of that lands in a T1/T2 source, the penetration evidence would support raising confidence to high. AUM is preliminary month-end AUM at 30 June 2026.

rationale: Amundi's own chief operating officer, Guillaume Lesage, states that “All our employees have access to our ALTO Studio platform and half of them use it on a weekly basis” and that “We already have 20 real applications to asset management” — of which the single named example is compliance software “which allows a marketer to check that their proposal is compliant” (company claims: both statements are first-party and no independent T1/T2 source corroborates them at that magnitude). Stops short of scaling: the only disclosed penetration figure is weekly rather than daily use by about half of staff, exactly one of the claimed 20 applications is named in any fetched source, the agentic layer is described by Lesage as “the latest development to come”, which METHODOLOGY §4 counts as intent rather than deployment, and no fetched T1/T2 source names AI a formal strategic priority — Amundi's February 2026 full-year results release does not mention AI at all.

Excluded under METHODOLOGY §1(a): Amundi Technology's ALTO platform (ALTO Investment, ALTO Wealth & Distribution, ALTO Asset Servicing) and the AI engines Lesage says Amundi plans to offer to ALTO clients from the second half of 2025 are software Amundi sells to third-party managers, banks and wealth platforms — only statements about Amundi's own staff using ALTO Studio were counted toward the stage. The AM Tech Day award page does not itself disambiguate whether the Compliance Assistance tool is internal or a client module; the internal attribution rests on WatersTechnology calling Alto Studio Amundi's “internal data platform” with 500 users at the firm, and on Lesage's marketer example. name: Citadel
rationale: Citadel LLC — the multi-strategy hedge fund, distinct from the separately run market maker Citadel Securities — has at least two named AI systems in production for investment staff. The internally built Citadel AI Assistant, a chatbot trained on licensed data including transcripts, regulatory filings, brokerage research and the firm's own strategies, was reported in December 2025 to surface risks, generate tailored research and create reading lists aligned to an investor's portfolio, and to see regular use across almost all of the firm's equities investors (company claim, via CTO Umesh Subramanian); by May 2026 Head of Core Engineering Atte Lahtiranta described analysts using Claude for Excel to build and update coverage models, separate signal from noise and pressure-test their work (company claim). Both disclosures explicitly retain human authority — Subramanian cautioned that investment decisions remain for humans — which is precisely the augmentation constraint that defines scaling. Stops short of embedded: no public evidence of investment decisions taken without a human in the loop and no disclosed redesign of the organisation around AI; confidence is held at med rather than high because the single penetration figure is a company claim scoped to equities investors rather than the whole multi-strategy firm, and citadel.com returned 403 on every page tried, so no first-tier own-domain corroboration could be read.
footnote: Scope and sourcing calls. Citadel Securities, the electronic market maker, is a separate firm and none of its material was counted here; note that the Anthropic page names only "Citadel" without disambiguating the two, so that event is attributed to the hedge fund on the strength of the speaker's role and the investment-research content of the quote (coverage models, separating signal from noise), while the Hedgeweek event is unambiguous (equities investors, portfolio managers). Excluded under METHODOLOGY §1(b): Citadel's 2026 acquisition of the bulk of the equity book of the AI-focused fund Situational Awareness is an investment position, not operational adoption. Excluded on tier: the widely circulated "~$71B AUM" and "close to full adoption across stock-picking teams" figures trace to Business Insider and its republishers (Yahoo Finance), which is third-tier here and cannot be a sole source, so this row takes both its AUM and its penetration language from Hedgeweek instead. Also excluded on tier: an eFinancialCareers interview with Umesh Subramanian describing portfolio managers interacting with Citadel's AI tools via chatbot and roughly a decade of machine-learning use, which is third-tier and corroborates only. Pre-2023 quantitative and machine-learning history informs context but is not an event here.
